name: Diplodocus
fact: Diplodocus carnegii is 33 meters long — the longest sauropod with a complete skeleton. Its whip-like tail had 73 vertebrae.
know: The steel magnate Andrew Carnegie paid for the dig and then gave plaster copies of “Dippy” to museums in London, Berlin, Paris and other capitals — which is why it became the most-seen dinosaur skeleton in the world.
taxonomy: Dinosauria › Saurischia › Sauropodomorpha › Sauropoda › Diplodocoidea › Diplodocidae
discovery: First fossils discovered 1877 by S.W. Williston. Othniel Charles Marsh named genus in 1878.
keyResearchers: Marsh, O.C. (1878), Hatcher, J.B. (1901), Lacovara et al.
citation: Marsh, O.C. (1878). Principal characters of American Jurassic dinosaurs. American Journal of Science 16:411–416.

name: Brachiosaurus
fact: Standing 12 meters tall and weighing 80 tonnes, it was a living skyscraper. Modern biomechanical analysis shows it browsed the highest tree canopies.
know: The towering skeleton in Berlin, long shown in books as Brachiosaurus, is now classed as a different animal, Giraffatitan. The true North American Brachiosaurus is known from much less complete remains.
taxonomy: Dinosauria › Saurischia › Sauropodomorpha › Sauropoda › Macronaria › Brachiosauridae
discovery: First described 1903 by Elmer S. Riggs from fossils in Colorado River valley.
keyResearchers: Riggs, E.S. (1903), Janensch, W. (1914), Upchurch & Barrett (2000)
citation: Riggs, E.S. (1903). Brachiosaurus altithorax, the largest known dinosaur. American Journal of Science 15:299–306.

name: Stegosaurus
fact: Modern biomechanical analysis shows the tail spikes were weapons, capable of inflicting serious wounds on predators.
know: An Allosaurus tail bone has a hole punched through it that fits a Stegosaurus tail spike exactly — and the wound had begun to heal. The spikes were weapons, and they worked.
discovery: First described 1877 by Othniel Charles Marsh. Better specimen described 1879 at Como Bluff, Wyoming.
keyResearchers: Marsh, O.C. (1877–1879), Lull, R.S. (1910), Carpenter, K. (1998)
citation: Marsh, O.C. (1879). Notice of new Jurassic reptiles. American Journal of Science 17:513–514.

name: Allosaurus
fact: Top predator of the Jurassic! Unlike T-Rex, it had long arms with three sharp claws like giant hatchets it used to slash prey. It may have hunted in packs to bring down giant sauropods.

name: Archaeopteryx
fact: Its feathered skeleton perfectly bridges dinosaurs and birds. Modern consensus recognizes A. lithographica and A. siemensii as valid taxa.
know: The first skeleton was found in 1861, two years after Darwin predicted that links between major groups must have existed. It has a bird's feathers and wishbone with a reptile's teeth, clawed fingers and long bony tail.
discovery: First specimen reported 1861 in Solnhofen limestone, Bavaria. Described 1863 by Richard Owen.
keyResearchers: Meyer, H.v. (1862), Owen, R. (1863), Huxley, T.H. (1868)
citation: Owen, R. (1863). On the Archaeopteryx of von Meyer. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 153:33–47.

name: Rhamphorhynchus
fact: A pterosaur with a long tail and needle teeth for snatching fish. Pterosaurs weren't dinosaurs — they were flying reptiles that lived alongside dinosaurs but were their own totally separate group.

name: Plesiosaurs
fact: A marine reptile with four flippers and a long neck for stabbing fish. NOT a dinosaur, but ruled the seas while dinosaurs ruled land. The Loch Ness Monster myth comes from old plesiosaur fossils!

name: Compsognathus
fact: The tiniest known dinosaur! About the size of a chicken. Probably hunted small lizards and insects. Shows that dinosaurs came in many sizes, not just giants. The smallest dino we know of.

name: Camarasaurus
fact: The most common sauropod found in North America and the best-understood large dinosaur of the Jurassic. Its spoon-shaped teeth could strip tough vegetation that more delicate sauropods avoided. Camarasaurus fossils often show evidence of disease and injury, giving scientists a detailed picture of dinosaur health.

name: Megalosaurus
fact: The very first dinosaur to be scientifically named - in 1824 by William Buckland in Oxford, England. Its description launched the entire science of paleontology. For decades every large theropod bone found in Europe was called Megalosaurus, making it a wastebasket taxon scientists spent 150 years untangling.
know: The first dinosaur ever to be named, by William Buckland in 1824 — eighteen years before the word “dinosaur” existed. A piece of one had been illustrated as early as 1677, and taken for the thigh bone of a giant human.

name: Dimorphodon
fact: An early pterosaur with a disproportionately huge puffin-like head and a long tail tipped with a diamond-shaped steering vane. Dimorphodon could walk on all fours on the ground as well as fly, and likely caught fish and large insects along Jurassic coastlines.

name: Liopleurodon
fact: A powerful pliosaur with four massive flippers and jaws over 1.5 meters long. It could smell prey from kilometers away by sampling water through its nostrils. A BBC documentary famously and incorrectly depicted it at 25 meters long.

name: Kentrosaurus
fact: An African cousin of Stegosaurus with an extreme arrangement of alternating plates and spines running from neck to tail tip. Found in Tanzania it proves stegosaurs were global. Computer modeling shows it could swing its tail spines with enough force to shatter bone.

name: Dilophosaurus
fact: The real Dilophosaurus had no neck frill and spat no venom — both were invented for Jurassic Park. It was also about three times longer than the film's version: the largest land animal in North America in its day.
know: The first skeletons were found in 1940 by Jesse Williams, a Navajo man, on Navajo Nation land in Arizona. A full restudy in 2020 showed its jaws were strong, not weak, and its paired crests were honeycombed with air pockets.

name: Cryolophosaurus
habitat: Cool forests near the South Pole
fact: The first meat-eating dinosaur discovered in Antarctica, dug from rock 4,000 m up a mountain only 650 km from the South Pole. Its crest sweeps across the head like a pompadour, which earned it the nickname “Elvisaurus”.
know: Antarctica was not icy then. Fossil tree trunks and leaves in the same rocks show forests growing at high latitude through months of winter darkness.

name: Massospondylus
fact: A common plant-eater of early Jurassic southern Africa — and the owner of the oldest dinosaur nursery known: at least ten nests, laid in the same place over many seasons about 190 million years ago.
know: Embryos still curled in their eggs were scanned with a particle-accelerator X-ray beam. They had no working teeth and oversized heads, so the hatchlings probably could not feed themselves — a hint of parental care.

name: Heterodontosaurus
c: Dinosaurs › Early dinosaurs › Early bird-hipped dinosaurs
fact: Almost every reptile has one kind of tooth. This turkey-sized dinosaur had three: nipping teeth at the front, grinders at the back — and a pair of long tusks in between.

name: Scelidosaurus
c: Dinosaurs › Armoured dinosaurs › Early armoured dinosaurs
fact: An early armoured dinosaur studded with hundreds of bony plates — and the first nearly complete dinosaur skeleton ever found, in 1858. Its carcass had floated out to sea and sunk into the mud.
know: Richard Owen, who coined the word “dinosaur”, described it in 1861 and then left it. A complete scientific description was finally published in 2020 — almost 160 years later.

name: Mussaurus
size: Adults 6–8 m; hatchlings fit in a hand
means: Mouse lizard — named from its tiny babies
fact: More than 100 eggs and 80 skeletons from one breeding ground in Patagonia show Mussaurus lived in herds — and that the young kept together in their own age groups.
know: It is the oldest evidence of herd living in any dinosaur, 40 million years earlier than the next. X-ray scans of the eggs found embryos inside, proving whose nests they were.

name: Shunosaurus
fact: A short-necked sauropod with a surprise at the end of its tail: a bony, spiked club. It is the most common dinosaur at the Dashanpu quarry, where over 8,000 bones were found during construction of a gas-company car park.

name: Huayangosaurus
fact: One of the earliest stegosaurs. Unlike its later cousin Stegosaurus, it still had teeth at the front of its mouth and its plates were more like spikes — a snapshot of the group before it settled on its famous look.

name: Kulindadromeus
c: Dinosaurs › Early dinosaurs › Early bird-hipped dinosaurs
fact: A small plant-eater with scales on its tail and shins — and three different kinds of feather-like fuzz on the rest of its body.
know: All the feathered dinosaurs found before it were meat-eating theropods. Kulindadromeus sits on the opposite branch of the dinosaur family tree, which suggests some kind of feathering may go back to the very first dinosaurs.
debate: Whether its filaments are true early feathers or something that evolved separately is still argued.

name: Guanlong
fact: An early cousin of T. rex — 95 million years older, a twentieth of the weight, with long three-fingered arms and a thin, showy crest along its snout.
know: Two were found one on top of the other in a pit of soft volcanic mud that began as the footprint of a giant sauropod. Small dinosaurs blundered in and could not climb out.

name: Anchiornis
fact: A crow-sized dinosaur with long feathers on its arms and its legs — four wings. It lived about 10 million years before Archaeopteryx, the famous “first bird”.
know: In 2010 it became the first dinosaur to have its whole-body colours worked out. Microscopic pigment capsules in the fossil feathers were compared with those of living birds: grey body, white wing feathers tipped with black, and a rusty-red crest.

name: Yi qi
means: Strange wing (Mandarin) — the shortest dinosaur name
fact: A feathered dinosaur with wings of skin, like a bat. A long rod of bone grew from each wrist to help stretch the membrane — something seen in no other dinosaur.
debate: Could it flap, or only glide? Model tests suggest it was a clumsy glider at best: an experiment in flight that birds soon out-competed.

name: Mamenchisaurus
size: 22–26 m; neck up to about 15 m
fact: Half of this animal was neck. With 19 neck vertebrae — more than any other sauropod — one species had the longest neck of any animal known, about 15 metres.
know: CT scans show the neck bones were up to 77% air, like a bird's — light enough to hold out without collapsing.

name: Yangchuanosaurus
fact: China's answer to Allosaurus, and the top predator among the long-necked giants of Jurassic Sichuan. The first skeleton was spotted by a construction worker building a dam in 1977.

name: Ceratosaurus
fact: A hunter with a blade-like horn on its nose, a horn over each eye, and a row of small bony plates down its back — armour found on no other meat-eating dinosaur.

name: Apatosaurus
fact: A massively built sauropod with a neck far wider and heavier than a Diplodocus's. Its tail tapered to a thin lash; computer models suggest it could crack like a bullwhip, the tip breaking the speed of sound.

name: Brontosaurus
fact: Yes — Brontosaurus is back. Named in 1879, it was folded into Apatosaurus in 1903 and for a century the name was officially wrong.
know: In 2015 a team compared 477 anatomical features across 81 sauropod skeletons. Brontosaurus came out different enough from Apatosaurus — a higher, narrower neck among other things — to stand as its own genus again.
debate: Not every sauropod specialist accepts the split; how different is “different enough” is a judgement call.

name: Giraffatitan
fact: The skeleton in Berlin's Museum für Naturkunde stands 13.27 m tall — the tallest mounted dinosaur in the world. For most of a century it was called Brachiosaurus, until a 2009 study showed the African animal was a different genus.
know: Between 1909 and 1913 about 500 Tanzanian workers excavated the Tendaguru hill and carried some 250 tonnes of bone on foot to the coast, four days' walk away.

name: Supersaurus
fact: One of the longest dinosaurs known from good skeletons — longer than three school buses, with a neck of about 15 metres. Its shoulder blade alone is 2.4 m long.

name: Torvosaurus
fact: Heavier than Allosaurus and with blade teeth 10 cm long, Torvosaurus was the biggest predator of its world. The Portuguese species is the largest land predator ever found in Europe.

name: Europasaurus
fact: A dwarf sauropod. Its relatives weighed 30 tonnes; Europasaurus, marooned on an island where food was limited, weighed less than a cow.
know: Small bones could just mean young animals. But thin slices under the microscope show tightly packed growth rings at the edge — these were adults that had stopped growing.

name: Ornitholestes
fact: A light, long-fingered hunter that lived in the shadow of giants, probably catching lizards, small mammals and hatchlings. Only one good skeleton has ever been found, in 1900.

name: Pterodactylus
fact: The first pterosaur known to science, described in 1784 — when it was guessed to be a sea creature that paddled with its long arms. It is not a dinosaur: pterosaurs were a separate group of flying reptiles.
know: In 1801 the French anatomist Georges Cuvier recognised that the enormously long fourth finger supported a wing. No animal alive flies that way; bats use four fingers, birds use feathers.

name: Leedsichthys
means: Leeds's fish, after collector Alfred Leeds
fact: The largest bony fish that ever lived — and a gentle one. Like a whale shark, it cruised with its mouth open, straining plankton through tens of thousands of fine gill rakers.

name: Sinraptor
fact: A big Chinese hunter related to Allosaurus. Its skull carries healed bite marks from another Sinraptor.

name: Monolophosaurus
fact: A meat-eater with a single hollow crest running from its nose to above its eyes.

name: Eustreptospondylus
fact: One of the most complete large meat-eating dinosaurs from Europe — found in sea-floor clay, so its body must have washed out to sea.

name: Limusaurus
fact: Babies had teeth; adults had none. Limusaurus lost all its teeth as it grew up and switched to a beak — a change never seen in any other animal with a backbone.
know: Nineteen skeletons of different ages, found trapped in mud pits made by the footprints of giant sauropods, showed the teeth disappearing step by step.

name: Epidexipteryx
size: About 25 cm without the tail feathers
fact: Pigeon-sized, with four long ribbon feathers on its tail — for display, not flight. It could not fly at all.

name: Barosaurus
fact: Its neck was even longer than Diplodocus's. The American Museum of Natural History mounts one rearing up to defend its young — a pose that is still debated.

name: Omeisaurus
fact: A long-necked giant from Sichuan, named after Mount Emei, a sacred mountain in China.

name: Turiasaurus
fact: The largest dinosaur ever found in Europe, with heart-shaped teeth. Its upper arm bone alone is about 1.8 m long.

name: Lufengosaurus
fact: An early long-necked plant-eater — and the source of the oldest organic remains known.
know: In 2017, scientists found traces of collagen protein inside a 195-million-year-old rib. Normally only minerals survive that long.

name: Gargoyleosaurus
fact: One of the earliest ankylosaurs — armoured, but without the tail club its descendants would carry.

name: Miragaia
fact: A stegosaur with 17 neck bones — more than most sauropods — giving it a surprisingly long neck.

name: Tuojiangosaurus
fact: A Chinese stegosaur with 15 pairs of pointed plates down its back and four tail spikes.

name: Gigantspinosaurus
fact: A small stegosaur with enormous spikes sticking out from its shoulders — almost as long as its legs.

name: Dryosaurus
fact: A fast, slender plant-eater that relied on speed to escape Allosaurus.

name: Camptosaurus
fact: A bulky plant-eater that could walk on two legs or four — an early member of the line leading to the duck-billed dinosaurs.

name: Ophthalmosaurus
fact: Its eyes were 22 cm across — among the largest for its size of any animal. Big eyes mean dim light: it probably dived deep after squid.

name: Temnodontosaurus
fact: A giant ichthyosaur with eyes up to 26 cm across, and teeth for big prey — including other ichthyosaurs.

name: Pliosaurus
fact: A short-necked sea monster with a skull up to 2 m long. A near-perfect skull was pulled from a Dorset cliff in 2022.

name: Metriorhynchus
fact: A crocodile that went fully to sea, swapping legs for flippers and growing a fish-like tail fin.

name: Darwinopterus
fact: Half old-style pterosaur, half new: the body and tail of early pterosaurs with the head and neck of later ones.
know: One female was found with an egg — so we know which skeletons are female, and that females lacked the head crest.

name: Sordes
fact: Its name means “filth”: its fossil showed a coat of hair-like fuzz, evidence that pterosaurs were warm-blooded.

name: Castorocauda
fact: A beaver-like swimmer with a flat tail and fur, from the time of the dinosaurs. Mammal relatives were already trying many ways of life.

name: Juramaia
fact: A shrew-like climber possibly on the branch leading to placental mammals — which would make it a very distant ancestor of yours.
debate: Some argue the rocks are younger than first thought, or that it belongs elsewhere on the mammal tree.

name: Oligokyphus
fact: A weasel-shaped plant-eater with gnawing front teeth and a gap behind them, like a rodent. Tritylodonts were the last of the proto-mammals.

name: Kayentatherium
fact: A beaver-sized proto-mammal found with at least 38 babies — far more than any mammal has in one litter. Mammals later traded big litters for bigger brains.
know: The babies were spotted years after the block was collected, when a preparator noticed tiny teeth; CT scans then revealed the whole clutch.

name: Sinoconodon
c: Mammals › Mammal forerunners › Earliest mammal relatives
fact: It had the new, mammal-style jaw joint — but still grew all its life and replaced its teeth many times, like a reptile. Mammal features arrived one at a time.

name: Megazostrodon
fact: A shrew-sized insect-eater that probably came out at night, when the dinosaurs were less active. Small, furry and warm: the mammal plan for the next 130 million years.

name: Hadrocodium
c: Mammals › Mammal forerunners › Earliest mammal relatives
fact: As light as a paperclip, with a big brain for its size. Its ear bones may already have been separate from the jaw — the last step to a mammal’s ear. One of the smallest mammal relatives ever found.

name: Docofossor
fact: A Jurassic “mole” with shovel-like hands and short fingers for digging, strikingly like a living golden mole — evolved 160 million years ago.

name: Maiopatagium
fact: A glider with skin stretched between its arms and legs, preserved as a dark outline in the rock. Mammal relatives took to the air long before bats.

name: Volaticotherium
fact: A furry glider with a skin membrane, like a flying squirrel — but not related to any living glider.

name: Fruitafossor
fact: A digger with strong arms and peg-like teeth without enamel, like an armadillo’s — built for eating termites and ants in the time of Stegosaurus.

name: Lesothosaurus
c: Dinosaurs › Early dinosaurs › Early bird-hipped dinosaurs
fact: A small, fast, two-legged plant-eater from the very start of the bird-hipped dinosaurs — the group that later produced Stegosaurus and Triceratops.

name: Vulcanodon
fact: One of the first true sauropods: already on four pillar legs, but small. It was found between two lava flows by Lake Kariba, which help date it.

name: Patagosaurus
fact: A long-neck of Middle Jurassic Patagonia, known from many skeletons of young and old — so we can watch it grow up.

name: Brachytrachelopan
fact: A sauropod with a short neck — shorter than its back. It probably grazed close to the ground, like a giant cow.

name: Dicraeosaurus
fact: A short-necked sauropod with tall, forked spines along its neck and back, found at Tendaguru beside Giraffatitan — two giants feeding at different heights.

name: Elaphrosaurus
fact: “Light lizard”: a long, slender theropod from Tendaguru, known from almost everything except its skull. Its tiny arms and long legs suggest a fast runner.

name: Barapasaurus
fact: “Big-legged lizard”: one of the earliest giant long-necks, known from six animals that seem to have died together in a flood.

name: Rhoetosaurus
fact: Australia’s first well-known long-neck, found by a stockman in 1924. Its foot bones show it walked on a padded heel, like an elephant.

name: Eoabelisaurus
fact: The earliest known member of the short-faced abelisaurs. Its arms were already shrinking — a hundred million years before Carnotaurus ended up with arms smaller than a T. rex’s.

name: Piatnitzkysaurus
fact: A medium-sized hunter of Jurassic Patagonia, one of the best-known meat-eaters from the southern continents at a time when most fossils come from the north.

name: Spinophorosaurus
fact: One of the most complete early sauropods, found in the Sahara. Children from a nearby village helped dig it out.
debate: Two spiky bones found with it were first placed on the tail as weapons. They are now thought to be collar bones.

name: Afrovenator
fact: “African hunter”: a light, long-armed predator known from one nearly complete skeleton — rare for an African meat-eating dinosaur.

name: Glacialisaurus
fact: “Frozen lizard”: a long-neck dug from a mountain 4,000 m up and 650 km from the South Pole. Antarctica was forested then, though the winter nights lasted months.

name: Kileskus
fact: One of the oldest known relatives of Tyrannosaurus, from Siberia — a modest hunter with a nose crest, 100 million years before its giant cousin.
